questions.question: Who was Rama Natha?
options: The son of a rich landlord
questions.explanation: The story introduces Rama Natha as the son of a rich landlord.

questions.question: What did Rama Natha’s father leave him?
questions.explanation: His father left him large areas of land, but Rama Natha did not initially care for them.

questions.question: What did Rama Natha believe the potion could do?
questions.explanation: Rama Natha was fascinated by the idea of a potion that could turn things into gold.

questions.question: Why was Madhumati worried?
options: Rama Natha was spending too much money on the potion search
The sage had taken their land
questions.explanation: Madhumati feared that their money would soon run out.

questions.question: Who told Rama Natha how to collect dew?
questions.explanation: Mahipati gave Rama Natha instructions that required patient work.

questions.question: What was Rama Natha told to do to obtain the dew?
options: Grow banana plants, care for them and collect morning dew by hand
Wait for the sage to bring it
questions.explanation: The sage’s plan required Rama Natha to tend banana plants and gather dew himself.

questions.question: How much dew did Rama Natha need to collect?
questions.explanation: The sage set five litres as the amount to be collected.

questions.question: How did Madhumati help create the family’s wealth?
options: She asked the king for coins
She turned the dew into gold
She took the banana crop to the market and sold it
questions.explanation: Madhumati sold the bananas and obtained a good price for the crop.

questions.question: How long did it take Rama Natha to collect the five litres?
questions.explanation: The story says that he finally had five litres after six years.

questions.question: What did Mahipati want Rama Natha to understand?
options: Hard work, not magic, had created the family’s wealth
questions.explanation: The plantation and the sale of fruit—not a magic potion—produced the wealth.

questions.question: What does “potion” mean in “A Bottle of Dew”?
options: A liquid believed to have magical properties
A small branch of a tree
questions.explanation: A potion is a liquid believed to have magical effects. Rama Natha hopes it will turn ordinary objects into gold.

questions.question: What is dew, as defined in the story?
options: A liquid used to polish wood
Small drops of water that form on leaves at night
Water kept in a river all day
questions.explanation: Dew forms when water vapour condenses into tiny droplets on cool surfaces. In the story, the droplets are gathered from banana leaves in the morning.

questions.question: What is a plantation in the story?
options: A large area where plants or crops are grown
A storage space under a roof
questions.explanation: A plantation is a large area of land used to grow crops. Rama Natha’s banana plants eventually become a source of income.

questions.question: What does “tended” mean in “He tended them carefully”?
questions.explanation: To tend plants is to look after them by providing care. Rama Natha must tend the banana plants patiently.

questions.question: What does “muttered” mean in the story?
questions.explanation: To mutter is to speak quietly, often so the words are not easily heard.

questions.question: Which word is closest in meaning to “precious” in the story?
questions.explanation: Precious means valuable or greatly valued. Rama Natha thinks the dew is important because he associates it with the hoped-for potion.

questions.question: What does “wisdom” mean in the story’s ending?
questions.explanation: Wisdom is good judgement or deep understanding. Rama Natha learns from experience that steady work creates real value.

questions.question: What does the phrase “give up” mean in the story?
questions.explanation: To give up means to stop trying. Rama Natha continues gathering dew over a long period.

questions.question: Who is a sage in the story’s vocabulary activity?
questions.explanation: A sage is a wise person, often respected for knowledge and judgement. Sage Mahipati guides Rama Natha towards the lesson of hard work.

questions.question: What does “large tracts of land” mean?
questions.explanation: A tract is an area or stretch of land, so “large tracts of land” means large areas of land.

success should come instantly without effort
people should avoid learning from mistakes

options: In the shade of a neem tree in her courtyard

questions.question: How old does Neem Baba say the tree family is?
questions.explanation: Neem Baba says it was born millions of years ago.

questions.question: Where does Neem Baba say the tree may have originated?
questions.explanation: The conversation identifies North India or Myanmar as possible origins.

questions.question: In which broad regions can neem be found according to the text?

questions.explanation: Neem Baba says the family spread to many Asian and African countries and parts of America.

questions.question: Which Sanskrit name is mentioned for neem?
questions.explanation: Arishta is one of the Sanskrit names mentioned.

questions.question: Who is said to have given the tree the name Neem?

questions.question: Which parts of the neem tree does the passage say can be used to make medicines?

questions.explanation: The text names several parts of the tree as useful in preparing medicines.

questions.question: How can neem seed powder help protect crops according to the text?
options: It makes crops grow without water
It turns all insects into birds
When mixed with water and sprayed, it can keep some crop-damaging pests away
It replaces the need for sunlight
questions.explanation: The passage describes neem seed powder as a way to deter locusts and other crop pests.

questions.question: Which is one everyday use of neem mentioned in the dialogue?
options: Neem oil is used to make soaps and toothpaste
Neem wood is used to make glass
Neem leaves are used to write letters
Neem seeds are used as coins
questions.explanation: The dialogue lists soaps, toothpaste and other household uses.

questions.question: What does “thought-provoking” mean in “Neem Baba”?
questions.explanation: Thought-provoking describes something that makes a person think deeply. The conversation encourages Amber to consider a tree’s uses.

questions.question: What are twigs?
questions.explanation: Twigs are small, thin branches growing from a larger branch or stem.

questions.question: What does “breed” mean in the passage about germs and insects?
questions.explanation: Breed means to reproduce or produce young; for germs and insects it refers to multiplying.

questions.question: What is stagnant water?
options: Water stored in a closed bottle only
questions.explanation: Stagnant water is water that is not flowing. It may provide a breeding place for some insects.

questions.question: What does “cost-effective” mean in Amber’s comment?
options: Giving a good outcome with few resources
questions.explanation: Cost-effective means achieving a useful result without excessive cost or resource use.

questions.question: What does “purifies” mean in the passage?
options: Makes cleaner by removing harmful particles
questions.explanation: Purifies means makes cleaner or removes impurities. It does not mean that a plant makes every substance completely safe.

questions.question: Which meaning is given for the Sanskrit name “Arishta”?
options: A tree that grows only in cold places
The name of a village officer
questions.explanation: In the textbook’s explanation, Arishta is associated with curing disease. This is a traditional name meaning, not a guarantee that neem cures every illness.

questions.question: Which Hindi name does Neem Baba give for the neem tree?
questions.explanation: The passage gives “Nimb” as a Hindi name for neem. This checks the name used in the textbook dialogue.

questions.question: What caution does Neem Baba give about remedies?

questions.explanation: Neem Baba advises that remedies should be used only by people who are properly trained and experienced.

Their names appear before their lines
questions.explanation: In a dialogue, a speaker’s name appears before that person’s words, helping the reader follow the conversation.

questions.question: What did the young bird think the world was like in its first little house?
options: A large lake made of water
Small, round and made of a pale blue shell
questions.explanation: The first stanza describes the bird’s early, limited view of the world.

questions.question: Where did the bird live next?
options: Inside a cage in a market
questions.explanation: The poem says the bird next lived in a little nest.

questions.question: What did the bird think the world was made of while in the nest?
questions.explanation: The bird believed the world was made of straw because that was its nest.

questions.question: Who was with the bird in the nest?
questions.explanation: The poem says the bird nestled by its mother.

questions.question: Why did the bird flutter from its nest?
options: To search for a magic potion
To buy food at the market
To escape a storm described in the poem
To see what it could find
questions.explanation: The bird leaves its nest to explore the world.

questions.question: What did the bird think after leaving the nest and seeing leaves?
options: That the world was made of feathers
That the world was made of leaves
That the world was made of gold
That the world was a river
questions.explanation: The bird’s view changes when it sees leaves outside the nest.

questions.question: What happens when the bird flies beyond the tree?
options: It learns that its neighbours know everything
It discovers the full shape of the earth
It returns to the blue shell
It is ready for grown-up tasks but still does not know how the world is made
questions.explanation: The final stanza shows growth without complete knowledge.

questions.question: What does the bird say about its neighbours’ knowledge?
options: They do not know how the world is made either
They have never seen a tree
questions.explanation: The final line says the neighbours do not know either.

questions.question: What is a central idea of the poem?
options: A bird can understand everything at once
The smallest home is always best
Experience can broaden our view, but we may still have questions
questions.explanation: The bird’s understanding changes as its experience grows.

questions.question: How is the poem told?
options: In the first person by the bird
As a letter from a grandmother
questions.explanation: The poem repeatedly uses I to present the bird’s thoughts.

questions.question: What does “pale” mean in the description of the bird’s shell?
questions.explanation: Pale means light or not strong in colour. It describes the shell’s soft blue appearance.

questions.question: What does “fluttered” mean in the poem?
questions.explanation: Fluttered means moved with light, quick movements. It helps the reader imagine the bird’s movement.

questions.question: What does “at length” mean in the poem?
questions.explanation: At length means eventually or after some time.

questions.question: What does “labour” mean in the poem?
questions.explanation: Labour means work or effort. In the poem it refers to exertion, not a job title.

questions.question: Which word is an adjective describing the bird’s first world?
questions.explanation: Round is an adjective describing the shape of the bird’s first world.

questions.question: Which pair rhymes in the first stanza?
questions.explanation: “Well” and “shell” rhyme because their ending sounds match.

questions.question: Which word signals the bird’s first-person voice?
questions.explanation: “I” is a first-person pronoun, signalling that the bird tells the experience from its own point of view.

questions.question: What does “I have been very blind” suggest in the poem?
options: The bird had not understood the wider world
The bird cannot see any colour at all
The bird has hurt its wing
The bird has lost its nest forever
questions.explanation: The phrase suggests the bird’s earlier understanding was limited. Exploring the wider world changes its perspective.

questions.question: In the final stanza, who are the bird’s neighbours?
questions.explanation: Neighbours are people or beings nearby. In the poem, the word refers to others around the bird.

questions.question: What is a stanza?
options: A group of lines forming one section of a poem
A word that means the opposite
questions.explanation: A stanza is a group of lines forming a section of a poem, much like a paragraph in prose.

questions.question: Which idea best captures the central theme of “What a Bird Thought”?
options: experience can broaden understanding beyond the small world we first know
personal fame matters more than helping others

questions.explanation: The phrase conveys how dusk changes what the children see.

questions.explanation: The line playfully treats night as the winner because play must stop.

questions.question: Which mood best fits the poem?
options: Energetic and playful, then aware of evening
questions.explanation: The poem captures the excitement of play and the arrival of night.

questions.question: What does the poem celebrate?
options: The pleasure of energetic outdoor play
questions.explanation: The poem focuses on the joy and excitement of children playing outdoors.

questions.question: What is a creek in “The Winner”?
questions.explanation: A creek is a small stream or narrow body of flowing water. The children play in a neighbour’s field beside it.

questions.question: What does “catch my breath” mean in the poem?
questions.explanation: To catch one’s breath means to recover normal breathing after physical effort. The line shows how hard the children have been running.

questions.question: What does “When blue dark turns to black” describe?

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which reading approach best identifies a central idea?
options: Look for the idea connecting several important details

questions.explanation: A central idea connects important details.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: How should a reader support an interpretation?
options: Use a long word without explaining it
State the interpretation and point to a relevant detail
questions.explanation: Textual evidence strengthens an interpretation.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which question asks about motivation?
options: How many letters are in the title?
Why does the character choose this action?
How many paragraphs are on the page?
questions.explanation: Motivation concerns the reason behind an action.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which choice is an inference?
options: A fact quoted word for word
A conclusion drawn by combining clues in the text
questions.explanation: An inference is a reasoned conclusion from clues.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: What makes a summary effective?
options: It states the main ideas without minor details
questions.explanation: A summary condenses important content without inventing information.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which is an opinion rather than a fact?
options: It is the most enjoyable chapter in the book
questions.explanation: “Most enjoyable” expresses a personal judgement.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: What should a reader do with an unfamiliar word?
options: Use surrounding clues and reread the sentence
Assume it is a proper noun
questions.explanation: Context clues can help readers infer meaning.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: How should two characters be compared?
options: Compare their actions, motives and responses
Assume they are alike because they appear together
questions.explanation: A useful comparison uses evidence from the text.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: What does tone describe?
options: The attitude or feeling conveyed by the writing
The number of words per page
questions.explanation: Tone is conveyed by language and detail.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which detail is best evidence for a claim?
options: An unrelated fact about the reader
A specific action or statement connected to the claim
questions.explanation: Evidence connects directly to a claim.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: What does setting describe in a narrative?
options: Where and when the events occur
questions.explanation: Setting identifies time and place.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: What can a title help readers anticipate?
options: The topic, a key image or an important idea
questions.explanation: A title signals the text’s focus.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which transition word signals a result?
questions.explanation: “Therefore” introduces a result.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: How can a reader check an answer?
options: Return to the relevant section and compare it with the text
questions.explanation: Returning to the text verifies the answer.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which question is open-ended?
options: Which word is in the title?
How do the key events develop the theme?
How many lines are in the stanza?
questions.explanation: Open-ended questions invite explanation.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: What is the purpose of a concluding sentence?
options: To bring the paragraph back to its main point
To repeat the opening word for word
questions.explanation: A conclusion reinforces the paragraph’s focus.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which choice shows a fair interpretation?
options: Describe what the text supports and avoid claims beyond its evidence
Ignore details that disagree with your view
Treat an opinion as a fact
questions.explanation: A fair interpretation is grounded in evidence.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Which strategy identifies cause and effect?
options: Look only at the number of characters
Find words with the same first letter
Ask what happened and what action or event led to it
questions.explanation: Cause and effect links actions or events to results.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: Why distinguish fact from opinion?
options: To make every sentence a question
To separate verifiable information from personal judgement
To decide opinions are always wrong
questions.explanation: Facts can be checked; opinions express judgements.

questions.question: Reading skills applied to “National War Memorial”: What should a strong paragraph include?
options: A clear point, relevant evidence and an explanation
Only a quotation with no context
questions.explanation: A claim, evidence and explanation make analysis convincing.
